name: Contouring injection surgery (fat removal)

card.summary: A family of Korean-style and clinic procedures, from fat-dissolving injections to buccal fat removal, that take volume out of the lower face to define cheeks, jawline and chin.
card.note: Fat removal is permanent; only one injectable (deoxycholic acid, for under-chin fat) is FDA-approved for fat reduction.

quick.overview:
Facial contouring by fat removal aims to slim the lower face so the cheekbones, jawline and chin read sharper. Options range from injections that dissolve fat, such as deoxycholic acid for the area under the chin, to minor surgery such as buccal fat removal, where a small pad of fat is taken from each cheek.

Filler studies often sit in the same clinics: separate trials test hyaluronic acid and calcium hydroxylapatite fillers for jawline contour, which add volume rather than remove it. Evidence for fat-dissolving injections is mostly retrospective; one product has regulatory approval for the chin area.
quick.how: In clinics, a practitioner marks the area and either injects a fat-dissolving drug over several sessions or, for buccal fat removal, removes fat through a small incision inside the mouth, usually under local anesthesia in about 30 minutes. Swelling settles over days and final results may take up to three months.
quick.risks: Buccal fat removal can injure facial nerve branches or the parotid duct, and the loss is permanent, so cheeks may look hollow with age. Unapproved fat-dissolving mixtures have drawn FDA warning letters, and reports describe scarring, deformation and painful lumps. Kybella commonly causes swelling, bruising and numbness.

lead: Contouring by fat removal covers procedures meant to slim parts of the lower face. Practitioners and patients, including many in the Korean aesthetics market, use injections that destroy fat cells or small surgeries that remove fat to sharpen the jawline, chin and cheek hollows.[1] For people who are already lean but whose face still looks round, the appeal is that these procedures change the fat that diet and exercise do not reach, so the cheekbones, jaw angle and neck line read more clearly.

Two procedures dominate. Injection lipolysis uses drug mixtures, usually phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate, in many small injections over several sessions to destroy fat cells.[3] Buccal fat removal takes a small portion of the buccal fat pad from each cheek through an intraoral incision to reduce cheek fullness.[4] The only fat-reducing injectable approved by the FDA is deoxycholic acid (Kybella), approved April 29, 2015 for moderate-to-severe fat below the chin.[5]

Buccal fat removal in particular became a social media and celebrity topic in the early 2020s, after actress and model Chrissy Teigen disclosed having had it in 2021, and it is a recurring subject on looksmax.org, with threads on results, hesitation, regret, consensus and do-it-yourself attempts.[4][6][7][8]

chain: Remove or dissolve fat in cheeks or under the chin
More visible cheekbone, jawline and neck angle
angle.text: These procedures reduce fat that obscures bone and muscle contours. People choose them for a slimmer, more angular lower face when diet alone does not change facial fullness.

paras: Injection lipolysis mixes drugs, often phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate, which are injected under the skin in many small doses across multiple sessions to destroy fat cells.[3] Deoxycholic acid injected into submental fat breaks down fat cells, which the body clears over several months.[5]

Buccal fat removal is a cosmetic surgery removing a small piece of the buccal fat pad from each cheek, typically under local anesthesia with the patient awake. The surgeon makes an incision inside the mouth near the upper second molar, separates the fibers of the buccinator muscle, and teases out and removes the fat; the procedure takes about 30 minutes. It generally has no medical benefit, so insurance seldom covers it.[4] It is often done alone but can be combined with a facelift, chin implant, neck lift, chin liposuction or fat grafting.[4]

Recovery typically involves swelling for a few days that is often not visible from outside, with dissolvable stitches, and final results can take up to three months.[4] Cost varies widely: Wikipedia cites a RealSelf average of $4,097 in 2023, while surgeons interviewed in 2022 quoted from $7,000 up to $16,000, and a medical tourist was reported to have paid $600 in Tijuana in 2020.[4]

The buccal fat pad was described by Lorenz Heister in 1732 as glandular tissue and identified as fat by Xavier Bichat in 1802.[4] Interest rose after Chrissy Teigen revealed in 2021 that she had the procedure; in 2022 The New York Times reported its rising popularity on Twitter and TikTok, quoting a surgeon who called it one of the classic celebrity secret plastic surgeries, and the American Society of Plastic Surgeons counted 4,543 procedures in 2022, its first year tracking it, making it the least common facial technique on its list.[4] Social media gave it the nickname Handsome Squidward surgery, after a chiseled-faced character from SpongeBob SquarePants.[4]

Injection lipolysis traces to the discovery in 1966 that intravenous phosphatidylcholine solutions could clear fat emboli. A formulation of phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate, Lipostabil, was approved in Germany for fat embolism, dyslipidemia and alcohol-related cirrhosis, and a 2001 report described injecting it to remove fat under the eyes. Studies by Rotunda and colleagues in 2005 and 2006 examined deoxycholate-based injections for fat.[3] In 2015 the FDA approved deoxycholic acid for double chin; a generic version became available in the US in April 2021.[3][5]

Deoxycholic acid is a bile acid the body uses to emulsify fats for absorption in the intestine. When injected into submental fat it acts as a detergent-like agent that destroys fat cells, which the body then clears over several months.[5] It is sold as Kybella in the US, where it is prescription-only, and as Belkyra in Australia, where it is a Schedule 4 medicine; Kybella was produced by Kythera Biopharmaceuticals.[5]

Buccal fat removal risks include injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve (possible numbness, partial paralysis or loss of taste) and to the parotid duct (saliva collections). The removal is permanent, and long-term effects have not been well studied. Because cheeks naturally lose volume with age, removing fat may later make a person look gaunt, although fat injections, dermal fat grafts and fillers can mimic or restore volume.[4]

In April 2010 the FDA sent warning letters to six U.S. medspas and a Brazilian company over 'lipodissolve' claims, stating the products were not approved for fat removal and reporting adverse effects such as permanent scarring, skin deformation and painful knots. The American Society of Plastic Surgeons, the American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery and the American Society of Dermatologic Surgery have issued warnings, and the UK's MHRA told physicians such drugs could not be promoted for fat reduction.[3] Wikipedia reports no placebo-controlled studies showing the mixtures are safe or effective, with efficacy claims resting on retrospective Lipostabil studies.[3]

In German-speaking countries the approach is used widely. Lipostabil N has been approved in Germany for more than 40 years, and a physicians' group reported safety data from about 29,889 patients across roughly 76,000 sessions, although only 4 percent of members responded to the survey.[3] Kybella's reported side effects include swelling, bruising, numbness and, rarely, nerve injury.[3]

Forum threads include success stories ('saved my mental health'), questions about whether a 24-year-old with chubby cheeks should do it, requests for tips, reports of results with photos months later, and discussions on whether removal replaces getting lean.[2][9][10][11][15] In one thread an original poster with a babyface at around 15 percent body fat asks how risky the surgery is; a reply says a conservative surgeon will typically reduce rather than fully remove the fat and recommends a partial removal.[10] A thread titled as a 'perfect hardmaxx or the worst mistake' reflects the split in opinion about it, and others ask whether bloating or facial fat can be addressed first.[12][16]

Members on looksmax.org discuss buccal fat removal alongside the broader hardmaxx toolkit of jaw implants, rhinoplasty and facial filler. The threads also include self-performed attempts that appear in forum titles, which clinicians generally describe as carrying the risks listed above without a surgeon's supervision.

A 2017 Radiographics review covered soft-tissue procedures in plastic surgery, including contouring by liposuction, fat grafting and injections, from the perspective of how they appear on imaging.[1] Wikipedia describes injection lipolysis as lacking placebo-controlled studies, while deoxycholic acid for submental fat is the product with regulatory approval.[3][5]

Registered filler trials on jawline contour test volume addition rather than fat removal, which people sometimes combine with slimming to change the jaw's outline: Radiesse in 180 participants (NCT03583359), a Radiesse jawline study in 29 participants (NCT02904057), a filler jaw-contouring study in 14 participants (NCT06694857) and a trial of LANLUMA V in 192 participants.[13][14][17][18]

timeline.event: Lorenz Heister describes the buccal fat pad.[4]
Xavier Bichat identifies it as fat.[4]
Researchers find intravenous phosphatidylcholine can remove fat emboli, the origin of later injection lipolysis.[3]
Report describes under-eye fat removal with Lipostabil injections.[3]
Rotunda and colleagues begin publishing on deoxycholate injections for fat (studies in 2005 and 2006).[3]
FDA warning letters to U.S. medspas and a Brazilian company over lipodissolve claims.[3]
FDA approves deoxycholic acid (Kybella) for under-chin fat.[5]
Chrissy Teigen discloses buccal fat removal; interest rises; generic deoxycholic acid becomes available in the US.[4][5]
ASPS begins tracking buccal fat removal, recording 4,543 procedures; The New York Times reports its rise on social media.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, buccal fat removal is treated as a hardmaxx option for people who are lean but still have full lower cheeks.[6][7][8]

claims.claim: Buccal fat removal sharpens the face when getting lean does not
claims.believers: Posters describe starving and heavy cardio without changing facial fullness, then credit the surgery and leanness with improving their confidence.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the procedure as cosmetic, with no medical benefit, and notes that final results take up to three months.[4]

claims.claim: A conservative, partial removal ages well
claims.believers: Replies advise a partial removal and a conservative surgeon who reduces rather than removes the fat.[10]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that cheeks lose volume with age, so removal may later look gaunt, and that long-term effects are not well studied.[4]

claims.claim: Removal replaces the need to get lean
claims.believers: Threads ask whether the procedure makes leanness unnecessary for facial definition.[11]
claims.experts: No studies have compared surgery against weight loss for facial contour.

claims.claim: Fat-dissolving injections can slim the face safely
claims.believers: Clinics and users describe repeated small injections as a non-surgical option for fullness.[3]
claims.experts: The FDA says lipodissolve products are not approved for fat removal and reported scarring, deformation and painful knots; only Kybella is approved, and only for submental fat.[3][5]

claims.claim: Buccal fat removal is a permanent fix
claims.believers: Posters see permanence as the advantage over fillers, which fade.[2][12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia confirms permanence, with fillers or fat grafting as ways to restore volume later.[4]

claims.claim: Self-performed removal is a workable alternative to a surgeon
claims.believers: A forum thread titled as a self-performed removal shows photos of the result.[19]
claims.experts: Surgeons describe risks to the facial nerve branches and parotid duct.[4]
